idiom_name: injected strategy object used by the lock statement (System.Threading.Lock on .NET 9, otherwise Monitor), ReaderWriterLockSlim for reader/writer policies
implementation_notes: The strategy is any object the component locks on: since .NET 9 and C# 13 the dedicated System.Threading.Lock type is the recommended one, and the lock statement recognizes it and compiles to Lock.EnterScope(), whose returned ref struct disposes to exit the scope - Scoped Locking supplied by the runtime. On older targets Monitor (object-based lock) and ReaderWriterLockSlim (EnterReadLock/EnterWriteLock/EnterUpgradeableReadLock) provide the mutex and reader/writer policies, and the component holds whichever strategy it was given instead of a hard-coded lock object. C# monitors are re-entrant, so the classic self-deadlock force is weaker here, but the performance and policy arguments still apply; a component with one forever-fixed policy is simpler with a plain lock.
pitfalls: lock(this), lock(typeof(T)) or locking a string literal publishes the strategy to foreign code, which can then take the same lock; ReaderWriterLockSlim must never be the target of a lock statement (it is a policy object, not a monitor).

ReaderWriterLockSlim is not re-entrant by default - recursion requires the LockRecursionPolicy constructor that the documentation advises against for new code; use EnterUpgradeableReadLock instead of nested read/write acquisition.

ReaderWriterLockSlim and Lock are IDisposable: the owned strategy must be disposed with the component, and a monitor cannot be held across an await at all (SemaphoreSlim is the asynchronous mutual-exclusion primitive).
